articles.title: The case for learning everything a little badly
articles.excerpt: Specialists go deep, generalists connect the dots. Why being a master of none often beats being a master of one.
articles.author: eric

children.text: The full proverb is longer than most people remember: a jack of all trades is a master of none, but oftentimes better than a master of one.
Breadth is a skill
Knowing a little about a lot is a different kind of expertise: recognizing patterns across fields and borrowing solutions from one to fix problems in another.
Depth tells you how. Breadth tells you where to look.
Start badly, on purpose
Every new thing you pick up will be clumsy at first. Pay that price often enough and you stop being afraid of being a beginner.

articles.title: I self-hosted my whole stack in a weekend
articles.excerpt: One VM, a reverse proxy, and a lot of coffee. What went right, what broke at 2 a.m., and what I'd change.
articles.author: dana

children.text: Friday night I had three subscriptions and no idea where my data lived. By Sunday I had one server and a plan.
The setup
A single virtual machine, Docker Compose, and a reverse proxy handling HTTPS.
$ docker compose up -d
What broke
DNS, of course. It is always DNS.

children.text: Where it started
Every project on this blog starts the same way: curiosity, a little too much confidence, and no real plan. This one was no different.
What I learned
The details will be different for you, but the pattern holds. Start small, write things down, and expect the first attempt to be the practice run.
You do not need to be an expert to begin. You become one, a little, by beginning.
